newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Gazprom set to drive Russian stock market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gazprom set to drive Russian stock market.

text.p: Russian gas monopoly Gazprom said it would become a locomotive for the domestic stock market on Friday as it closed the door on foreign investors who would not play by its rules.

Gazprom officials said a presidential decree which would come into force when published would support high prices of Gazprom stock trading abroad by stopping majority foreign-owned companies from buying cheap local shares.
But the new decree will not force foreigners currently holding local shares to sell and allows a loophole for foreign investors to buy into mutual funds with limited Gazprom stock.
"The rules for trade on the domestic market have been spelled out well enough," Alexander Semenyaka, Gazprom's board member in charge of securities, told a news conference.
"Holders of American Depositary Shares (ADSs) have been assured that the two-tier system will be maintained."
Foreigners are required to hold Gazprom in the form of ADSs, share look-alikes which trade abroad but cost about triple the price of the local shares which Russians buy.

Gazprom's ADS, covering 10 local shares, rose to $18.100 at 1535 GMT in London after $18.075 at the close on Wednesday. Shares in Moscow on the Russian Trading System (RTS) fell to $0.6050 after $0.6495.
The prices of the ADS had languished since its launch last year as many foreigners circumvented restrictions by establishing Russian-registered subsidiaries which legally bought local Gazprom shares.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell estimated such grey market ownership at seven percent or more of Gazprom equity.
Semenyaka dismissed fears that its strict rules would be circumvented by investors eager to avoid high international prices. "Long-term capital does not try to get around the law."
First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov was quoted as saying he expected ADS prices to jump five or six times.
Semenyaka said shares would jump when Gazprom released results of an audit of gas reserves being prepared.
Semenyaka said Gazprom, comfortable with the new restrictions, expected to become a leading proponent of order in the Russian stock market.
Gazprom maintains a right of first refusal to buy its shares but will give up the right on "organised markets" included on a list the government will draw up.
The over-the-counter type RTS is the largest stock market but may not be named an organised market unless it meets criteria which Gazprom officials said they would help draw up.
Gazprom will give up completely its right to first refusal in 1999.

Semenyaka said a nine percent cap on foreign ownership could end at that point. The cap is mandated during the privatisation period when the government holds 40 percent of Gazprom shares, which it must do until 1999.
Semenyaka also said Gazprom had allowed a loophole for Russian mutual funds to allow foreign investment, which Semenyaka said would boost the Russian economy.
The decree allows mutual funds, which may be invested in by foreigners, to hold 10 to 20 percent of its assets in Gazprom.
"To invest one dollar in Gazprom, you have to invest nine dollars in the Russian economy, on the stock market," Semenyaka said.
